title: The Haunted Man and the Ghost’s Bargain
author: Charles Dickens
setting: An old college hemmed in by the streets of London, a newsvendor's house in Jerusalem Buildings and a lodging-house under a viaduct, from twilight on Christmas Eve to Christmas dinner the next day
lengthNote: About 33,000 words in three chapters: The Gift Bestowed, The Gift Diffused and The Gift Reversed
summary: Redlaw, a famous chemist who lives alone in an old London college, is haunted by the memory of a neglected childhood, a friend who took the woman he loved, and a sister who died. On Christmas Eve a phantom with his own face offers to cancel his memory of sorrow, wrong and trouble, and he accepts. The gift spreads to everyone he meets. Tenderness, gratitude and forgiveness go with the painful memories: a loving family turns sour, an old man disowns his dying son, a grateful student insults his nurse. Only two people are proof against it: a starving boy who has never had a kind memory to lose, and Milly Swidger, the keeper's wife, whose own grief has made her kind.
referenceStyle: chapter, as Dickens numbered the book's three chapters

structure.label: Chapter I
structure.title: The Gift Bestowed
structure.summary: Redlaw sits alone at twilight in his room, part library and part laboratory, in an old college squeezed among the streets of London. William Swidger, the keeper, brings his dinner; William's wife Milly decorates the room with holly; William's father Philip, who is eighty-seven, remembers Christmases back to his childhood and repeats the prayer under the founder's portrait, Lord, keep my memory green. Milly mentions a sick, poor student in Jerusalem Buildings who will not let Redlaw help him. When they have gone a phantom in Redlaw's likeness recites his history and offers to cancel his memory of sorrow, wrong and trouble. He accepts, and is told that he will destroy the same memory in everyone he approaches. A ragged boy Milly has taken in runs into the room, and Redlaw finds he feels nothing for him.

scenes.title: The haunted man
scenes.summary: The narrator's portrait of Redlaw by his fire at twilight, while the shadows gather in the corners of the room.

scenes.title: The Swidgers
scenes.summary: William's praise of Mrs William, Philip's holly and his memory of the founder's portrait, and Milly's account of the student who is ill.

scenes.title: The bargain
scenes.summary: The Phantom tells Redlaw his own story, makes its offer and, once he has accepted, adds the condition that he will pass the gift on.

scenes.title: The boy
scenes.summary: A barefoot child with no name bursts in looking for the woman who fed him, and Redlaw looks at him coldly and sends him away.

structure.label: Chapter II
structure.title: The Gift Diffused
structure.summary: In the Tetterbys' crowded shop in Jerusalem Buildings, Mrs Tetterby confesses to her husband that she had wished she had never married, then remembered what their hard years have given them. Redlaw arrives looking for the student and touches Mr Tetterby, and when he looks back from the stairs the family has turned sullen and cold. The student, Edmund Denham, tells him that his real name is Longford: he is the son of the friend who wronged Redlaw. Under Redlaw's influence he turns on Milly. Redlaw then follows the boy, who alone is unchanged, to a lodging-house among the arches of a viaduct. There a young woman with a bruised face insists that nobody hurt her, and Philip and William are watching over William's elder brother George, who is dying. George begins to repent and warns that a ruined man upstairs means to kill himself; at Redlaw's approach George hardens, Philip disowns him, and William turns on his father. Back in his room, with Milly at the door begging for help, Redlaw calls on the Phantom to take the gift back.

scenes.title: The Tetterbys
scenes.summary: A newsman, his wife, their seven sons and a baby girl called Moloch; a quarrel, a confession and a reconciliation over a supper from the cook's shop.

scenes.title: The student
scenes.summary: Edmund's secret, Milly's muslin curtain, and the cold thanks that make her leave the room.

scenes.title: The lodging-house
scenes.summary: The woman on the stairs, George Swidger on a truckle-bed, and a broken man in the corner whom Redlaw cannot place.

scenes.title: The door
scenes.summary: Milly knocks and pleads to be let in while Redlaw holds the boy back and prays for the power to be undone.

structure.label: Chapter III
structure.title: The Gift Reversed
structure.summary: Towards dawn Christmas music reaches Redlaw and moves him to tears, and the Phantom returns, less cruel, holding the hand of Milly's shadow. It tells him he cannot undo the harm himself and must seek her out, and explains the boy: a child who has never had a humanising memory, the image of what Redlaw chose to become. In the morning the Tetterbys, still quarrelling, recover the moment Milly comes down the street, and Edmund begs her pardon. Milly has found the ruined man in time: he is Longford, Edmund's father and Redlaw's old friend, and Redlaw, who cannot remember the wrong, pays for him to go away and says he would forgive him if he knew for what. When Milly speaks of the baby she lost, Redlaw's memory returns. He vows to protect and teach the boy and gives a Christmas dinner for the Swidgers in the old hall, under the portrait.

scenes.title: The shadow of Milly
scenes.summary: The Phantom stands over the sleeping boy and speaks of the country's neglected children.

scenes.title: Mrs William is coming
scenes.summary: A morning of Tetterby quarrels ends when Johnny sees Milly in the street and picks the baby up tenderly.

scenes.title: Longford
scenes.summary: Milly brings in the ruined friend, and Redlaw forgives a wrong he can no longer remember.

scenes.title: The old hall
scenes.summary: Milly speaks of her child, Redlaw's memory returns, and the Swidgers dine by firelight beneath the founder's portrait.

characters.name: Redlaw
characters.role: A learned chemist and lecturer at an old London college
characters.summary: Famous for his chemistry and loved by his students, he lives alone with the memory of a neglected childhood, a friend who took the woman he loved, and a sister who died. The bargain leaves his learning intact and takes everything that made it humane. He grows cold, then frightened of himself, and spends the rest of the night trying to undo what he chose. By the end the learned man walks beside the keeper's wife as though their positions were reversed and she were the teacher.
characters.clue: He keeps every fact he has learnt, forgets why the sight of a starving child should hurt, and hides in a small back room to avoid a kind woman.

relationships.label: teaches, and later takes as a son

characters.name: The Phantom
characters.summary: An awful likeness of Redlaw that gathers out of the shadow behind his chair, with his features, his bright eyes and his grizzled hair. It tells his story in the first person and admits that its words are an echo of his own mind. It returns in the last chapter less cruel, holding the hand of Milly's shadow, and tells him to seek her out.
characters.clue: It leans on the back of a chair wearing a copy of the sitter's own face, and when asked whether the harm can be undone, it answers No.

characters.name: Milly Swidger
characters.role: The keeper's wife, called Mrs William
characters.summary: Small, quiet and neat, she mothers the students, nurses the sick student in secret, brings a starving boy home from a doorstep, and turns down Redlaw's purse. She lost a baby who lived only a few days, and says the memory has made her kinder to every child she sees. Her presence undoes the gift wherever she goes, though she has no idea she is doing it; when she tells Redlaw about her child, his memory comes back.
characters.clue: She trims holly with her scissors, stitches a muslin curtain for a sick lodger, and says of each new person who loves her, That's another.

characters.name: William Swidger
characters.summary: Fresh-coloured and always busy, he agrees with everyone before they have finished and prefaces most of what he says with That's what I always say. He is devoted to his wife and his father until the gift reaches him at his brother's deathbed, when he looks at his father and sees only a calendar of meals.
characters.clue: He names each thing as he sets the table, Pepper, Spoon, Bread, and claims the family could join hands in a ring round England.

characters.name: Philip Swidger
characters.role: William's father, custodian of the college for more than fifty years
characters.summary: He tells everyone that he is eighty-seven and remembers every Christmas since he was a small boy, including the one when his mother died. He knows the founder's prayer by heart. At his eldest son's deathbed he loses his memories and his love at once, disowns George and nibbles at a sprig of holly, and he recovers both when Milly comes home.
characters.clue: He goes round the old building every Christmas with an armful of holly, and asks everywhere, Where's my son William?

characters.name: Edmund Denham
characters.role: A poor student in Redlaw's class
characters.summary: Ill with a fever and too proud to go home or ask for help, he lodges above the Tetterbys' shop and is nursed by Milly. He has studied under an assumed name: he is the son of Longford, the friend who wronged Redlaw, and has kept away from his teacher out of shame and respect. Touched by the gift he treats Milly as a servant who wants paying; restored, he begs her forgiveness, and the young woman he is to marry arrives at the college to find him.
characters.clue: He keeps a framed engraving of his teacher in his room, and asks to be known only by the name he has taken, not by his father's.

characters.name: Longford
characters.summary: The friend who won the woman Redlaw loved, and whom Redlaw's sister also loved. He married her, left her and their son, gambled and sank, and is found in the lodging-house, penniless and meaning to kill himself. Milly traces him in time, and Redlaw, who can no longer remember the wrong, pays for him to go somewhere he can do no more harm.
characters.clue: He knows a little medicine, sits up with a dying stranger in a lodging-house, and asks to be forgiven by a man who cannot remember what for.

characters.name: George Swidger
characters.summary: His mother's favourite, he has wasted his life in vice and is dying on a truckle-bed in a lodging-house for travellers. His father's memories of him as a child begin to soften him, and he uses his last strength to warn that the man who brought his family will kill himself. Redlaw's presence hardens him; Milly's visit at sunrise brings him to repentance.
characters.clue: Told on his deathbed that his mother forgave him, he starts to repent, then covers his ears and says he has lived bold and means to die bold.

characters.name: The boy
characters.summary: About six years old, barefoot and in rags, found by Milly shivering on a doorstep. He has no name and does not know what it means to live anywhere. Redlaw's gift has no effect on him, and the Phantom explains why: nothing kind has ever happened to him that could be taken away. By the end Redlaw vows to protect and teach him, and he will stay only by Milly.
characters.clue: He threatens to bite if he is hit, keeps his shillings in his mouth, and asks for the woman.

characters.name: Mr and Mrs Tetterby
characters.role: A newsman and his wife in Jerusalem Buildings
characters.summary: Adolphus Tetterby, who trades as A. Tetterby and Co., Newsmen, has tried and failed at every line from sweets to tobacco. His wife Sophia is twice his size. They have seven sons and a baby girl, Sally, called Moloch, and they are loving and generous with very little. Touched by Redlaw's gift they find each other plain and their marriage a sacrifice; Milly's arrival in the street restores them.
characters.clue: He reads improving paragraphs off a screen pasted with newspaper cuttings; she turns her wedding ring round and round when something is wrong.

characters.name: Johnny Tetterby
characters.role: The Tetterbys' son and nurse to the baby
characters.summary: The small boy who carries the baby Moloch everywhere, staggering under her weight and missing everything worth seeing. Under the gift he slaps her and says he will go for a soldier because there are no babies in the Army; the moment he sees Milly coming he picks the baby up as tenderly as an old nurse.
characters.clue: He crushes himself on a stool under the weight of his baby sister and keeps his pudding in his pocket.

themes.name: The use of painful memory
themes.summary: The bargain rests on the idea that people would be happier without their memory of sorrow, wrong and trouble. Every scene after it tests that idea and finds it false: gratitude, forgiveness and love turn out to be made from the memories Redlaw gave away.
themes.development: Redlaw begins by calling memory his curse and ends by thanking Heaven for its return; the book's last words are the founder's prayer that his memory be kept green.

themes.name: Remembering in order to forgive
themes.summary: Milly's answer to Redlaw is that people should remember the wrongs done to them so that they can forgive them. A man who cannot remember a wrong can only pay for it; he cannot pardon it.
themes.development: Redlaw can offer Longford money and an abstract forgiveness in the third chapter, but the real forgiveness comes only after his memory returns.

themes.name: A child with nothing to lose
themes.summary: The boy is the one person on whom the gift has no effect, because nothing kind has ever happened to him. The Phantom makes him the book's social argument: a nation that leaves children to grow up like this will reap what it sows.
themes.development: Redlaw moves from disgust at the boy to seeing his own face in him, and finally to vowing to protect and teach him.

themes.name: Home and hardship
themes.summary: The Tetterbys have tried every trade and have eight children and little money, yet Mrs Tetterby comes to see their struggles as the thing that made them one. The book sets their crowded parlour against Redlaw's solitary, vault-like rooms.
themes.development: The gift reverses the Tetterbys' feelings overnight, and Milly's arrival restores them, with Mrs Tetterby finding 'the air of home' in her husband.

themes.name: Learning without feeling
themes.summary: Redlaw keeps all his knowledge and loses only the feelings bound up with his memories. The book asks what learning is worth when it is cut off from sympathy, and reverses the positions of the learned man and the uneducated woman.
themes.development: Redlaw reaches the truth through his own science, reflecting that in the material world no atom can be lost without a gap, and applies it at last to good and evil in memory.

themes.name: The poor as the book finds them
themes.summary: The characters live in a college lodge, a failing shop, a garret and a lodging-house for travellers under a viaduct. Dickens puts the destitute boy and the woman on the stairs in front of a learned man who has shut himself away from them.
themes.development: What begins as private grief becomes, in the Phantom's speech over the sleeping boy, a charge against every parent, every country and every religion that tolerates such children.

techniques.name: The double
techniques.definition: A figure who mirrors or embodies part of another character.
techniques.inThisBook: The Phantom has Redlaw's face and speaks his thoughts as an echo, and the boy's face comes to wear Redlaw's expression. The book dramatises a man bargaining with himself.

techniques.name: Refrains
techniques.definition: A phrase that recurs and gathers meaning each time.
techniques.inThisBook: Sorrow, wrong and trouble; the gift that I have given; Lord, keep my memory green; Philip's I'm eighty-seven. Each returns in a changed situation, and the last one closes the book.

techniques.name: Characters known by their speech
techniques.definition: A way of talking that belongs to one character.
techniques.inThisBook: William's That's what I always say, Philip's Where's my son William?, Milly's That's another. The phrases make the Swidgers comic, and their loss or distortion under the gift is how the reader sees the change.

techniques.name: The twilight catalogue
techniques.definition: A long list of parallel clauses building a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: The first chapter's run of sentences beginning When, from the city streets to ships at sea and children afraid of the stairs, slows the story down to the moment the shadows gather and the knock comes.

techniques.name: Holly and the portrait
techniques.definition: Objects that carry the book's meaning.
techniques.inThisBook: Philip's holly withers on Redlaw's wall as the Phantom appears, and the old man later nibbles at a sprig with no memory of why it matters. The founder's portrait, with its scroll, presides over the final dinner.

techniques.name: The narrator's reserve
techniques.definition: The narrator speaking in his own voice to the reader.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator opens by doubting what everybody says and closes by listing what people have said since about the story, before adding I say nothing, and then saying one thing more.

techniques.name: Balanced opposites
techniques.definition: Setting opposed ideas against each other in parallel phrasing.
techniques.inThisBook: The Phantom's verdict on the boy and Redlaw is built on two matched clauses, and Mrs Tetterby answers her husband by taking each of her unkind thoughts about him and turning it into a reason to love him.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: A gap between what is said or intended and what turns out to be true.
techniques.inThisBook: The gift is offered as a blessing and works as a curse, George's defiance is the sound of his repentance being taken away, and the learned man learns his lesson from a woman who says she does not know how to think properly.

quotations.text: Everybody said he looked like a haunted man.
quotations.context: The opening, after the narrator's doubts about what everybody says.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence of the book is Everybody said so, and this is what everybody said. Dickens lets the title come to us as gossip, and then spends two pages agreeing with it, so the reader meets Redlaw through his appearance before hearing him speak.

quotations.context: Philip describes the scroll beneath the founder's portrait in the old dinner hall.
quotations.analysis: An Elizabethan benefactor's prayer to be remembered after death. Philip applies it to himself, as a way of keeping his own past alive, which is exactly what Redlaw is about to give away. The book ends on the same words.

quotations.text: There’s a motherly feeling in Mrs. William’s breast that must and will have went.
quotations.context: William begins to tell Redlaw about his wife's latest kindnesses.
quotations.analysis: The grammar collapses under the weight of his admiration, which is the joke and also the truth. William cannot say why Milly mothers everyone, only that she must; the book supplies the reason at the end, a child she lost.

quotations.text: Thus, memory is my curse; and, if I could forget my sorrow and my wrong, I would!
quotations.context: The Phantom finishes reciting Redlaw's history in the first person.
quotations.analysis: Spoken by the ghost, the wish belongs to the man, which is why Redlaw cannot argue with it. The whole book is the testing of this one sentence.

quotations.text: I WILL forget my sorrow, wrong, and trouble!
quotations.analysis: Sorrow, wrong and trouble are the book's refrain, and the capital letters make the choice a matter of will rather than temptation. He has already argued that he would take an antidote for poison in his body; this is the same reasoning applied to the mind.

quotations.text: The gift that I have given, you shall give again, go where you will.
quotations.context: The Phantom's condition, announced only after Redlaw has agreed.
quotations.analysis: As in a fairy-tale bargain, the sting comes after the contract. Redlaw had asked what he himself would lose; he never asked what others would, and the rest of the book is the answer.

quotations.text: A baby savage, a young monster, a child who had never been a child
quotations.context: The narrator describes the boy who has rushed into Redlaw's room.
quotations.analysis: Each phrase is harsher than the last and each is qualified by his age. Dickens uses the language of horror for a six-year-old deliberately, so that the reader has to ask who made him so.

quotations.text: All our struggles for a livelihood, all our cares and wants since we have been married, all the times of sickness, all the hours of watching, we have ever had, by one another, or by the children, seemed to speak to me, and say that they had made us one
quotations.context: Mrs Tetterby tells her husband why she stopped wishing she had married someone else.
quotations.analysis: Everything she lists is a hardship, and every hardship is what binds them. It is Milly's argument made in a poor family's parlour before Redlaw arrives, and it is the thing his touch will take away a few minutes later.

quotations.text: but for some trouble and sorrow we should never know half the good there is about us.
quotations.context: Milly, sewing a curtain for Edmund, talks about his illness.
quotations.analysis: Trouble and sorrow are two of Redlaw's three words, and Milly gives them the opposite value. She says it with no idea that the man hiding in the next room has just given his away.

quotations.text: I am infected! I am infectious! I am charged with poison for my own mind, and the minds of all mankind.
quotations.context: Redlaw, having heard Edmund insult Milly, strikes him and runs out.
quotations.analysis: A chemist to the last, he reaches for the language of contagion. The antidote he wanted in the first chapter has turned out to be a poison he carries to others.

quotations.text: I have lived bold, and I mean to die bold.
quotations.context: George, who a moment before was asking whether there is hope for him, feels the gift reach him.
quotations.analysis: It sounds like defiance and is really loss: the memories that were bringing him to repentance have just been taken, and bravado is what is left.

quotations.text: In the material world as I have long taught, nothing can be spared; no step or atom in the wondrous structure could be lost, without a blank being made in the great universe.
quotations.context: Redlaw's prayer while Milly knocks at his door.
quotations.analysis: Redlaw finds his repentance in his own subject. He applies the conservation of matter to memory, and concludes that sorrow and wrong cannot be subtracted without leaving a gap.

quotations.text: He is the growth of man’s indifference; you are the growth of man’s presumption.
quotations.context: The Phantom explains why the boy has been proof against Redlaw's influence.
quotations.analysis: A balanced sentence that sets the two characters at opposite poles and then joins them. The boy is what neglect makes; Redlaw is what pride has made of himself; both have arrived at the same emptiness.

quotations.text: Woe, tenfold, to the nation that shall count its monsters such as this, lying here, by hundreds and by thousands!
quotations.context: The Phantom stands over the sleeping boy.
quotations.analysis: The ghost turns from Redlaw's private case to the country's. The word monsters picks up the narrator's description of the boy in the first chapter and throws it back at the reader.

quotations.text: I thought there was no air about you; but there is, and it’s the air of home, and that’s the purest and the best there is
quotations.context: Mrs Tetterby answers her husband's apology once Milly is in sight.
quotations.analysis: She repeats each unkind thing she thought and turns it round. The pun on air, meaning both manner and atmosphere, carries the whole reconciliation.

quotations.context: Milly's answer when she asks Redlaw why it is good to remember wrong done to us.
quotations.analysis: Five words from a woman who says she has no learning answer the learned man's reasoning of the first chapter. Forgetting a wrong makes it impossible to pardon.

quotations.context: The last words of the book, on the scroll under the portrait in the old hall.
quotations.analysis: The prayer returns without its exclamation marks and with Memory given a capital. After everything, it reads as a plain request rather than an old man's refrain.

criticalViews.position: A book about the value of painful memory
criticalViews.summary: Read as an argument, the story is carefully built: every character touched by the gift loses something good that depended on a bad memory, and Milly states the conclusion plainly.
criticalViews.counter: Milly is so good that she never has to be tested; the argument is proved by her, rather than worked out in her.

criticalViews.position: The social case rests on the boy
criticalViews.summary: The Phantom's speech over the sleeping child is one of Dickens's most direct statements about neglected children, and ties the book to the ragged-school campaigns of the 1840s.
criticalViews.counter: The ending answers it with one man's private promise to one boy, which is small beside the thousands the Phantom describes.

criticalViews.summary: With its double, its infection and its study of a mind cut off from feeling, the book is closer to a psychological ghost story than the earlier Christmas books.
criticalViews.counter: The Swidgers and Tetterbys are comic set pieces in the old style, and some readers find the two halves of the book do not join.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens show that memory of suffering is necessary?
plan: Begin with Redlaw's reasoning for the bargain, including the comparison with an antidote for poison.
Trace the effect of the gift on the Tetterbys, Edmund and the Swidgers, and what each loses.
Examine Milly's view that trouble teaches us the good about us, and her memory of her child.
Consider the boy as the proof: a person with no kind memories.
Conclude with the restoration and the final prayer.

essayQuestions.question: What is the Phantom?
plan: Describe how the Phantom first appears and what it looks like.
Examine its admission that it is an echo of Redlaw's mind.
Compare its cruelty in the first chapter with its milder return in the third.
Connect it with the boy, whose face comes to wear Redlaw's expression.
Argue whether the ghost is best read as supernatural, psychological or allegorical, using the narrator's closing reserve.

essayQuestions.question: How does the book connect private feeling with public responsibility?
plan: Set Redlaw's private grief against the poverty of Jerusalem Buildings and the lodging-house.
Analyse the Phantom's speech over the sleeping boy.
Consider the woman on the stairs and George Swidger.
Weigh the ending: Redlaw's vow and the Christmas dinner.
Conclude on whether the book's remedy matches the scale of the problem it describes.

discussionQuestions: Would you take the Phantom's offer? What would you lose?
Why are the boy and Milly the only two people the gift cannot reach?
What do the Tetterbys add to a ghost story about a chemist?
Redlaw forgives Longford before he can remember what Longford did. Does that count as forgiveness?
Is the Phantom evil, or only honest?
The narrator says 'I say nothing' about what really happened. What do you think happened?

related.why: The first Christmas book, where memory is also the way back to feeling.
The second Christmas book, another visionary night that turns on how the poor are treated.
The third Christmas book, a domestic story with a fireside spirit.
Another learned man who divides himself and cannot undo it.
